title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Japan: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Japan: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Japan: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: When a Japanese citizen dies in Japan, administrative duties begin with medical certification, municipal civil registration, and a mandatory 24-hour waiting period before cremation or burial, followed by pension, tax, and mandatory real property title filings. Because municipalities operate the Family Register (koseki) and issue cremation permits while national agencies administer pensions and taxes, keeping multiple certified copies of initial certificates prevents repeated office visits. This checklist summarizes the official sequence of actions based on current Japanese statutes and central government portals [1][2][5].

steps.title: Immediate medical certification and police clearance
steps.html:
• Hospital or attended death: The attending physician issues the Medical Certificate of Death (shibo shindansho), which shares the same official paper form as the Death Notification submitted to municipal offices [2].
  • Death at home or unexpected death: Under Japanese law and municipal practice, contact emergency services (119) or the local police immediately so a physician or medical examiner can investigate the cause of death and issue a Post-Mortem Examination Certificate (shitai kenansho) if foul play is excluded [2][10].
  • Keep copies before municipal surrender: Municipalities retain the original signed shibo shindansho or shitai kenansho once the death is filed, so make photocopies or ask the hospital for extra duplicates before submitting the form [2].

steps.title: Civil registration and obtaining official death records
steps.html:
• Seven-day statutory filing deadline: Under Article 86 of the Family Register Act (Koseki-ho), a relative or authorized informant must submit the Death Notification (shibo todoke) within 7 days of learning of the death (or within 3 months if a death occurs outside Japan) [1][2].
  • Filing office: Submit the Death Notification and attached medical certificate to the municipal office (shiyakusho, kuyakusho, or town/village hall) at the place of death, the deceased's registered domicile (honseki), or the notifier's address; Ministry of Justice (MOJ) Japan oversees the national koseki legal framework [1][2].
  • Certificate of Acceptance and updated koseki: Immediately request a Certificate of Acceptance of Death Notification (shibo todoke juri shomeisho) for pension, bank, and consular filings, and obtain an updated Family Register extract (koseki tohon or joseki tohon) showing the death entry once processing finishes [1][10].

steps.title: Body disposition permits, cremation, and Apostille authentication
steps.html:
• Statutory 24-hour rule and permit: Under Articles 3 and 5 of the Act on Graveyards, Burials, etc., cremation or burial may not occur until 24 hours after death (with statutory public-health exceptions), and requires a municipal Cremation or Burial Permit (kaso kyokasho / maiso kyokasho) issued when filing the Death Notification [4].
  • Cremation certificate and ashes transport: The crematorium stamps and signs the permit after cremation (maisou kyokasho), which is required to inter ashes in a cemetery or carry remains internationally alongside airline and destination-country documentation [4][10].
  • Hague Apostille for overseas use: Japan has been a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention since 27 July 1970, and Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan (MOFA) issues Apostilles free of charge for public documents bearing official municipal seals, or for private documents once notarized by a Japanese notary public (with One-Stop Service available at designated notary offices in Tokyo, Kanagawa, Osaka, and Fukuoka) [7][8][9].

steps.title: Social security, pension, tax, and household accounts
steps.html:
• Suspension and unpaid benefits: Report the death promptly to Japan Pension Service (JPS) (typically within 10 to 14 days for pension beneficiaries) to prevent overpayments and claim any Unpaid Pension Benefits (mikikyu nenkin) earned up to the month of death [5].
  • Survivors' and lump-sum pension claims: Depending on enrollment under the National Pension or Employees' Pension Insurance, eligible dependents may apply through Japan Pension Service (JPS) for Survivors' Basic Pension, Survivors' Employees' Pension, or the National Pension Lump-sum Death Benefit (shibou-ichijikin), while municipal offices administer the National Health Insurance funeral expense grant (sosaichi) [5][11][12].
  • Municipal and identity returns: Return the deceased's My Number Card, health insurance card, long-term care insurance card, driver's license, and passport (for cancellation) to the relevant issuing authorities, and submit the Quasi-Final Income Tax Return (jun-kakutei shinkoku) to the tax office within 4 months if the deceased was required to file [6][10].

steps.title: Estate administration, inheritance tax, and real property title
steps.html:
• Wills, statutory shares, and renunciation: Under Book V of the Civil Code, a will must be located and, unless executed as a Notarial Deed Will (kosei shosho yuigon) or held under the Ministry of Justice (MOJ) Japan Legal Affairs Bureau holographic will custody system, submitted to the Family Court for probate inspection (kennin); heirs have 3 months from learning of their inheritance right to apply to the Family Court to renounce an insolvent estate (sozoku hoki) [3][13][14].
  • Inheritance tax 10-month deadline: Where net taxable estate assets exceed Japan's basic exemption (30 million JPY plus 6 million JPY per statutory heir), National Tax Agency (NTA) Japan requires heirs to file and pay inheritance tax within 10 months of learning of the death, and non-resident heirs or estates with overseas assets may need a tax agent (nozei kanrinin) [6].
  • Mandatory real property inheritance registration: Effective 1 April 2024, heirs must register inherited real estate ownership with the Legal Affairs Bureau within 3 years of learning of the inheritance (with a compliance deadline of 31 March 2027 for properties inherited before 1 April 2024), or submit a simplified Heir Declaration to avoid a civil fine of up to 100,000 JPY [13].

contacts.note: Oversees the Family Register (koseki) system, Legal Affairs Bureau holographic will custody, and mandatory real property inheritance registration.

contacts.name: Japan Pension Service (JPS)
contacts.note: Administers death notifications, unpaid pension claims, Survivors' Pensions, and the National Pension Lump-sum Death Benefit.

contacts.name: National Tax Agency (NTA) Japan
contacts.note: Publishes official guidance on the 4-month quasi-final income tax return and the 10-month inheritance tax filing deadline.

contacts.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan (MOFA)
contacts.note: Designated Competent Authority under the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention; issues Apostilles without fee.
